items.caption: 268A. White moves. He has given up two Pawns to reach this promising combinative position. After 1 xe6, fxe6 he can regain one of the lost Pawns by 2 f4, attacking the Queen and King’s Pawn. But this pedestrian continuation is not good enough. After studying every check and capture, he plays 2 xe6+!

269A. Black moves. White’s centrally posted Bishop and Knight are insecure, as they are not guarded by Pawns. This calls for the powerful but fairly obvious 1 ... e8, striking at the Bishop and the pinned Knight behind it. 2 f4 is now forced, and play continues 2 ... xe4, this time forcing 3 xe4.

268B. Black moves. His King and Queen are attacked by the impudent, unprotected Rook, which must be captured. In the words of the Queen of Hearts, “Off with his head!” Black plays 2 ... xe6. But now White trumps this trick with 3 xg7+, an attractive Knight fork which wins the Queen.

269B. Black moves. White’s pinned Knight has disappeared, but his pinned Bishop is now the target. If 3 ... f6 White escapes by counterattack (4 a4). Study every check and capture! This yields the brilliant solution 3 ... c3+! forking King and Queen. 4 dxc3 is impossible; 4 xc3 loses White’s Queen.

270B. Black moves. He must capture the fatal Pawn, and either method of capture allows a pretty conclusion. Thus if 2 ... xe6; 3 e8+ wins Black’s Queen by the skewer. Or if 2 ... xe6 the newly unpinned Bishop asserts his freedom with the malevolent 3 c4, pinning (and winning) Black’s Queen. A deceptively simple position!

271A. Black moves. He wins a piece by combining three different ideas: Queen sacrifice, Knight fork and vulnerable first rank. This is all less formidable than it sounds. To begin with, he is dissatisfied with 1 ... f2+; 2 xf2, xf2 which merely wins the exchange. If only 2 ... e1+ were feasible! But White can interpose at f1. The solution: 1 ... xd3!!; 2 cxd3.

272A. White moves. Broken down into cold technical terms, his delightful combination makes use of a Queen sacrifice to seize the vulnerable last rank. There he pins a defended piece. Another pin, based on a sacrifice, removes the guard. Awe-inspiring as this may sound, the themes are old friends by now: :

273A. White moves. Zukertort, who had the White pieces here, was a “sugar-cake” in name only! He begins with the amazing Queen sacrifice 1 b5! The reply 1 ... xb5 is unavoidable, for if 1 ... d7?; 2 c8()+ or 2 xc6+ leaves White a Queen ahead. The combination unfolds with 2 c8()+, f7 (if 2 ... d8? the Knight fork c7+ wins the Queen).

272B. White moves. He must remove the guard of the pinned Bishop before Black can consolidate his defense. Therefore 3 xd5 pinning the Queen. Black is lost. He must play 3 ... xd5, else he loses the Queen. But now that the guard is removed, White plays 4 xe8 mate. Again we must admire the slick interplay of several combinative motifs.

273B. White moves. His next two moves should be seen in a flash by conscientious students of combination patterns. What can White obtain in return for parting with the precious Passed Pawn? The answer: 3 xe6+! xe6 and now the Knight fork 4 c7+ wins Black’s Queen. The upshot of the ingenious combination is that White has won a piece by forcing moves.

274A. White moves. His material advantage is enough to win, but he wants victory by the quickest route. Therefore he seeks forcing moves. The indicated target is Black’s f-Pawn, which is on an open file. So White begins with 1 e6. Black defends with 1 ... b7 and White adds more weight to the pin with 2 g6, forcing 2 ... f6.
275A. Black moves. His combination hinges on the fact that the two Queens are en prise to each other. He begins with a brutal move (and in chess one must be brutal):

276A. White moves. The beautifully intermeshed combination which follows is based on the fact that Black’s Bishop has to guard a Knight and the Queen (overworked piece!), and on the lack of communication between Black’s Rooks. Throughout, we seek checks and captures:

274B. White moves. Again on the lookout for violent moves, he breaks through with a sacrifice: 3 xf6+!, xf6 (if 3 ... g8; 4 f7 is decisive). After 4 xf6+ Black must play 4 ... e8 to guard his Rook at d8 from the double attack of White’s Queen. Now White winds up with a skewer: 5 h8+, e7; 6 g7+ (or 6 h7+) winning the Rook at b7.

277A. Black moves. His enormous advantage in position (based on the indirect pin by the Bishop) more than outweighs his material disadvantage. But to translate this into quick victory, he needs forcing moves. He begins with 1 ... xh2! If the Queen is captured (vulnerable first rank), 2 ... f1 mate.

277B. White moves. He plays 2 e1 (if 2 g1, Black has two ways of mating in two moves – how?). Black insists on sacrificing his Queen by 2 ... xe2+! Then if 3 xe2, f2 with double check and mate. Equally pretty is 3 xe2, f1 mate. Being pinned, White’s Rook must stay at e2.
278A. White moves. The Black Bishop is pinned! Hence the artistic move 1 f6! Black must not play 1 ... xf6 because of 2 e8 mate. So he tries 1 ... xc3, giving the Bishop more protection.
279. White moves. He has several ways of winning, but the quickest is based on a pin, followed by a Knight fork. How would you demonstrate this?
280. White moves. His modus operandi is a discovered attack followed by a Knight fork. What two moves does he play to bring this about?
281. White moves. He can win material by means of a double attack, followed by a pin. How?

295. Black moves. Classic position for smothered mate by Queen and Knight. (From a book by Lucena published in 1496!) The winning process after 1 ... h8 is 2 f7+, g8; 3 h6+, h8; 4 g8+!!, xg8; 5 f7 mate!

296A. White moves. All his pieces are trained on Black’s King-side. We see a mating pattern in the attack of Queen and Bishop against h7 (see Diagram 284). For the time being, this target is guarded by Black’s Knight. Therefore the Knight must be removed:

297A. White moves. He has an overwhelming attack, based partly on the fact that Black has moved the Pawns in front of his King. This weakness, plus the concentration of White’s forces, promises forceful sacrificial brilliancies to come. White’s Queen is attacked. Instead of retreating the Queen, he relies on the mating pattern of Diagram 292. There follows 1 xf6! Realizing that 1 ... xf6; 2 xh6 is quite hopeless, Black tries 1 ... gxh4.

298A. Black moves. His doubled Rooks are very powerful on the seventh rank. Were it not for the protective influence of the White Rook at g4, Black might be able to apply the mating pattern of Diagram 294. This automatically suggests a brilliant sacrifice: 1 ... xg4!; 2 fxg4.

297B. White moves. He must now prove the soundness of his Queen sacrifice. How? His Rook has a vital open file and is supported powerfully by the Bishop on f6. White plays 2 xg7+, which is answered by 2 ... f8 (if 2 ... h8; 3 g5 or 3 g4 or 3 g3 mate – the other Bishop also plays a role!). Now we are ready for the pattern of Diagram 292: 3 h7! No squirming can stop h8 mate.

299A. White moves. “White’s Knight is strongly posted at f5.” This comment, so often seen in annotations, introduces us to the pattern of Diagram 288. At this advanced post, the Knight offers ideal support for a checkmate with the Queen at g7. How is White’s Queen to get access to the vital square without loss of time? White plays 1 h6! discounting the fact that he leaves his Rook unguarded.

300A. White moves. The situation of his attacking forces (Knight on f6 and heavy pieces on the h- and g-files) reminds us irresistibly of the pattern shown on Diagram 293. The theoretically possible mates on h7 or g8 are both prevented by Black’s Rook at g7. The word both suggests that the Rook is overworked. And so it is: 1 xh7+!, xh7.

301A. White moves. He has sacrificed a piece, and can regain it if he wishes by 1 hxg6. But he seeks a more forceful line. The position calls to mind the pattern of Diagram 289 Accordingly White plays 1 h6+! renouncing the regain of the piece. The Pawn wedge establishes a powerful bind on the adverse King’s position.

299B. Black moves. As he cannot guard his g7, he snaps up the unprotected Rook. But after 1 ... xe1+; 2 f1, we perceive that the fate of the Rook was of no importance. What matters is that White, following the pattern for such positions, threatens 3 g7 mate. To prevent this mate, Black would have to give up his Queen with 2 ... e3+ – a fatal loss of material.

301B. Black moves. He gets out of check by 1 ... g8. Now comes 2 f6 and Black is helpless against 3 g7 mate. (The same position results from 1 ... h8; 2 f6+ etc.) In all these examples, the Queen is able to force mate at close range, supported by piece or Pawn. The hostile King cannot touch a piece that is protected.

302A. Black moves. The sweeping diagonal of his Bishop on b7 suggests the pattern of Diagram 292 – all the more so as Black has an open h-file. 1 ... h6 is too slow because of 2 f3, defending h2 and also closing the long diagonal. A violent move is needed: 1 ... xh2!

303A. White moves. He plays 1 h5, threatening 2 xh7 mate as in Diagram 287. Remember that the King is absolutely helpless to touch a piece which is protected. Black must play 1 ... h6 to prevent the mate. After 2 xg6 White again threatens mate at h7. White’s Queen is immune from capture, as. Black’s f-Pawn is pinned. Hence 2 ... hxg5 must be played.

304A. White moves. His Pawn at g6 reminds us of the mating pattern of Diagram 285. This calls for bringing the Queen to h7; but White’s Rooks are in the way, and he is also threatened with mate. He looks for violent moves:

302B. White moves. He is threatened with 2 ... h1 mate, as per pattern. White no longer has the defense 2 f3, for this would allow 2 ... xe2. White plays 2 xh2 and after 2 ... h6+ (2 ... h8+ also works); 3 g1 there follows 3 ... h1 mate. Applying the proper pattern made the Rook sacrifice a routine affair.

303B. White moves. His attempt to apply the pattern of Diagram 287 has been foiled. But there are other patterns! He plays 3 xg5, and the momentary threat against the Black Queen gains time for the attack. After 3 ... e8 White plays 4 f6! – with a beautiful double pin. The wedge with the Bishop forces mate (see the pattern of Diagram 290). Black’s pieces are paralyzed by pins.

304B. Black moves. These Rook sacrifices are becoming monotonous! Black must again capture, but after 4 ... xh8, the pattern of the desired mate has emerged in clear-cut form: 5 h1+ g8; 6 h7 mate. To complete his design for checkmate, White did not shrink from sacrificing two Rooks. His knowledge of the pattern he needed guided him to a victorious conclusion.

305A. White moves. Note how menacingly his Bishops are directed at Black’s King-side. Black’s Achilles heel is his g7, as White demonstrates with 1 g4. (1 d4 looks more natural, but allows Black to defend with ... g5). Black is now embarrassed for a defense to the threatened mate, as he cannot play 1 ... f6 (the Pawn is pinned!) nor can he play 1 ... f6.

306A. White moves. He has three pieces trained on Black’s King-side. If he retreats his attacked Bishop, Black will have time to consolidate the defense. Aiming for the pattern of Diagram 287, White plays 1 xh7+ Black replies 1 ... xh7. (Evasion by 1 ... h8 is pointless because of 2 h5.)

307A. White moves. The powerful position of his Queen and Bishop suggests the mating pattern of Diagram 284. But White must play the most exact moves. Thus 1 h7+ f8; 2 h8+ would allow Black to escape! The right way: 1 h7+, h8. Black’s King awaits his doom.

306B. White moves. He follows the pattern: 2 h5+, g8; 3 g5 threatening 4 h7 mate. As 3 ... xg5 would leave him hopelessly behind in material, Black prepares for flight with 3 ... d8. But “there ain’t no hidin’ place.” White winds up with 4 h7+, f8; 5 h8 mate. Another instance of the Queen’s powers.
